articles.title: State of emergency declared for California ahead of potentially historic El Niño
articles.summary: Gov. Newsom issued the proclamation to prepare California for coastal erosion, flooding, mudslides and winter storms.
articles.body:
Governor Newsom declares a state of emergency for California in preparation for a historic El Nino event.

The state of emergency mobilizes resources to support local mitigation and recovery efforts ahead of the anticipated severe weather impacts.

El Nino is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon caused by warming waters in the Pacific Ocean, with this year's event expected to be one of the strongest on record.

Gavin Newsom, the governor of California, declared a state of emergency for the entire state on Monday morning ahead of what is likely to become a historic El Niño.

"I find that conditions of extreme peril to the safety of persons and property exist due to the developing El Niño event," the declaration states.

This state of emergency is not an announcement that an emergency is already ongoing, but a statement of preparation for the storms that are ahead this winter.

The declaration mobilizes state-level resources to support local mitigation and recovery efforts, while streamlining the procurement of resources needed to prepare for El Niño's impacts.

"We are not waiting for this season's storms to be on our doorstep," said Cal OES Director Caroline Thomas Jacobs in a statement from the governor's office .

"Cal OES is leading California's statewide efforts by bringing state and local partners together, conducting advance planning efforts, and identifying potential needs before impacts occur. By planning early and coordinating resources ahead of El Niño, we are working to ensure communities and first responders have the personnel, equipment, and support they need to prepare for severe weather, respond quickly when conditions change, and protect lives and property across California."

El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon caused by warming waters in the Pacific Ocean. They typically occur every two to seven years. This year's El Niño is expected to be one of the strongest in historical record.

El Niño typically brings heightened chances of flooding, mud and rockslides, coastal erosion, and severe weather through relentless winter storms and atmospheric rivers.

You can also begin preparations for this impactful winter at your homes now.

Get your homeowner's insurance checked and make sure you have flood insurance . Any changes in policy can take up to 30 days to take effect.

This is not the first state of emergency related to El Niño, but it may be the first to be declared so early.

Two significant state of emergency proclamations were issued in previous El Niño events:

In January of the 1983 El Niño, several Southern California counties were placed under a state of emergency by then Gov. George Deukmejian following severe coastal damage and heavy rain. Additional storms hammered northern portions of the state leading to additional counties being put under a state of emergency.

Throughout February 1998's El Niño, then Gov. Pete Wilson issued, then expanded a state of emergency to 43 counties due to repeated storms.

Local state of emergency declarations have already been declared for this year's El Niño and Hurricane Marie's impacts in Orange County .

articles.title: 'I want to serve my country but I was rejected on health grounds'
articles.summary: Some 114,000 Army application were rejected on medical grounds in the past five years, Freedom of Information figures show.
articles.body:
Lewis Jackson cannot remember a time when he did not want to join the army and continue a family tradition of military service going back to World War One. That dream was shattered, though, when his application was rejected on medical grounds.

"Serving my country has always been a dream of mine and I never considered that I'd do anything else," said the 21-year-old.

Jackson, from Cirencester, was turned down by the Army because he had cataract surgery at the age of three.

A Ministry of Defence (MoD) spokesperson said: "Service in the Armed Forces is physically demanding, so it's right that we have sensible health and recruitment policies which maintain operational effectiveness but don't unnecessarily exclude people."

The BBC has spoken to potential recruits and professionals who question whether the rules are too strict while some applicants said they had been prevented from joining because of medical conditions they regard as minor or no longer relevant.

Jackson spent his teenage years in the Army Cadets where he was recognised in his unit as the best shot.

He applied to join the Army Reserve, motivated by a desire to "give back" to a country which he said had given him "so much", but he was rejected.

"It's very frustrating, especially when you know that you are fit and healthy and you haven't even been given the opportunity to fail," he said.

There were 108,020 applications to the British Army Regular Forces in the year leading up to September 2025.

Separate figures obtained under a Freedom of Information (FOI) request to the Ministry of Defence (MoD) showed more than 114,000 applications to the Army were rejected on medical grounds in the past five years.

Psychiatry, eye and musculoskeletal conditions were some of the most common reasons for rejection.

An MOD spokesperson said: "The majority of these figures cover years before the substantial changes the government has made to remove over 100 outdated and unnecessary recruitment policies."

The figures come against a backdrop of wider recruitment challenges for the armed forces.

Latest UK defence personnel report figures showed the military remained at about six percent below its full-time trained strength target with a shortfall of 8,460 personnel.

Jackson said he had appealed against the rejection, providing a range of supporting evidence, including a note from a consultant ophthalmic surgeon who said his vision was now "excellent in both eyes" and "everything was stable".

But although his vision now meets the standard, he is ineligible because medical entry rules mean applicants who have had lens replacement surgery are considered "unfit" as they need "the visual function to be able to perform their role safely and effectively".

He has been told he is "permanently medically unfit to serve".

Jackson said: "We are missing out on young men and women who are passionate about serving but instead are pursuing different careers.

"I think it is ludicrous. If you're fit, you should be able to join."

GP and Labour MP for Stroud Dr Simon Opher said there needed to be a "more sensible approach" to medical screening.

"If a health condition is stable and it's not affecting someone's functional ability, then there's no reason to exclude that person," he said.

"We have to get that balance right between what's happened in the past and what would actually affect an armed forces personnel in their day-to-day duties."

The MoD sets out the medical standards in a document known as the Joint Service Publication (JSP) 950 Medical Policy.

In 2024, it reviewed recruitment policies, including removing a ban on applicants with asthma and severe acne .

But for 20-year-old Ben Smith those changes have made little difference as his application was rejected because of ongoing use of an inhaler.

Smith, from Blandford Forum, Dorset, wanted to join the Royal Air Force (RAF) but asthma has prevented him from doing so.

"There is nothing more I wanted to do in the world," he said.

"I'd led 250 cadets on parades and then, for all of that to come crashing down when I didn't have a back-up plan, it was horrible."

After rising through the cadet ranks, Smith studied military protective services at college and dedicated himself to reaching the fitness standards required for service.

"I was lifting double my body weight in the gym and my bleep test scores were constantly improving."

Inspired by other family members who had served in the armed forces, he applied to join the RAF, hoping to train as either aircrew or a mechanic.

However, his application was rejected because he uses an inhaler.

Smith's appeal included a letter from his GP which said he had an "unlimited exercise tolerance".

The letter said: "He is a fit and active young man with a strong ambition to join."

The review said: "All candidates, irrespective of role, need to be a minimum of 12 months treatment, symptom and medication-free."

For Smith, the decision brought his life-long ambition to an end.

"I've been told no. I don't know what to do with myself."

Prof Neil Greenberg, president of the Society of Occupational Medicine, said: "The military has to have strict standards of physical and psychological health.

"It requires people to go all around the globe, often at short notice, and to put up with environments that really are quite unpleasant.

"It is vital that soldiers can perform to a very high level because if it goes wrong, it could mean loss of life."

Former British Army Lt Col Stuart Crawford, who was previously a defence spokesman for the Scottish National Party (SNP), said the military was "losing out on talent".

He said: "Recruitment policies must be in place, of course, but we need to be careful that we are not turning away talent because of minor medical issues."

He said this was "increasingly dangerous" in a time of global instability.

"We're always being told that we could be at war and we are nowhere near rising to that challenge in terms of our recruitment," Crawford said.

An MoD spokesperson said: "Each application is considered on a case-by-case basis by specialist clinicians, assessing the severity of any condition and the individual's ability to train, deploy and operate."

Jackson said the MoD needed to go "much further" in its review of recruitment policies.

"We're blanketing out thousands of young men and women," he said.

Jackson is currently studying agricultural management at the Royal Agricultural University in Cirencester.

"I'm in a lucky situation being at university where I have the time to fight my case alongside my studies," he said.

articles.title: The simple skincare routine for teens that actually works - and five expert tips
articles.summary: From popping spots to getting enough sleep, experts share their advice on the best way to look after teenage skin.
articles.body:
Social media is driving the trend for "flawless complexions" and complex "glass skin" routines in teenagers, with many prioritising advice from influencers in Get Ready With Me (GRWM) videos over professionals.

But do teens really need a multi-step skincare routine?

For consultant dermatologist Dr Jonathan Kentley, the most concerning influence social media is having is the "relentless images of unrealistic beauty standards".

"I've seen thousands of patients and I've never seen anyone with 'glass skin'. I don't think it exists, and it's just these over-filtered images that make children think that this is achievable when it's not."

Visible pores, blackheads, blemishes, pigmentation, redness and scarring are all very normal for teenage skin, says Dr Kentley. But he adds that everyone's normal is different: "I don't think there's anything that is really abnormal."

More than 80% of 13- to 18-year-olds experience acne during their teenage years.

Dr Zainab Laftah, a consultant dermatologist, explains that most of the so-called problems you encounter during puberty are related to testosterone, which drives rises in oil production and acne.

Boys can experience more of these problems, but girls have testosterone as well so get many of the same symptoms.

"This, together with blocked hair follicles and inflammation, leads to blackheads, whiteheads and inflamed spots," Dr Laftah says. "Acne is very, very common and it's normal and treatable."

Salicylic acid, a common active ingredient that penetrates into oil-filled pores to help clear the buildup of sebum and dead skin cells "can be particularly helpful for teenagers with oily or acne-prone skin" says Dr Laftah, warning that unnecessary or excessive use may cause dryness and irritation.

If you're suffering from severe acne or a severe skin problem, Dr Kentley advises getting help from your GP or a dermatologist rather than engaging with people on social media on how to manage it.

So, how best to look after teenage skin? Experts Dr Zainab Laftah and Dr Jonathan Kentley share their five top tips:

Keep your skincare routine simple You need three basics: a gentle cleanser, a fragrance-free moisturiser and a broad-spectrum sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher. That's it.

More skincare products aren't necessarily better A complicated routine with frequent exfoliations or strong acids can irritate young skin. Remember the skin barrier is still developing and it can result in damage. Dr Kently says he's seen an exponential rise in a condition called perioral dermatitis in teens, which is related to the overuse of ingredients that strip skin barriers like exfoliating hydroxy acids and retinoids. Dr Laftah adds: "Teens are increasingly adopting adult-style routines with numerous serums, toners, masks and actives. These actives are likely to result in skin barrier compromise and lead to more skin issues."

Getting enough sleep and a balanced diet is important Raised cortisol through diets high in white carbohydrates and sugar as well as a lack of sleep have been linked to breakouts. Dr Laftah is a supporter of getting a good night's sleep. "We know that a lack of sleep increases cortisol levels, which is a stress hormone that can lead to acne breakouts." While Dr Kentley says a diet that is high in carbohydrate foods, like white rice and pasta, high sugar diets and whey protein found in protein shakes have all been linked in studies to acne flare-ups. But he makes the point that everyone's skin is individual and that "some people may find that other things flare up their skin".

Don't pick or pop your spots The risk is that you can increase the inflammation by pushing the content deeper into the skin, which can result in scarring and discolouration. Dr Laftah says she's a fan of the pimple hydrocolloid star patches as a social media hack. "They work by absorbing fluid from superficial spots while creating a protective barrier that discourages picking," she explains.

See a GP or dermatologist If you have persistent painful cystic or scarring acne, seek medical advice, as often prescription-grade treatment is needed.

A lot of the so-called "problems" during teenage years are related to androgens, a hormone which, although present in girls, is more prevalent in boys.

"So male skin can sometimes be a little bit more oily and potentially have some more spots, and often you're getting to grips with the concept of facial hair and shaving, and that can introduce irritation," explains Dr Kentley.

"If you're not shaving properly you can develop quite a lot of folliculitis which is a bit of a crossover from acne. So you can cause quite a lot of damage to the skin barrier, a lot of inflammation."

Here are Dr Kentley's top tips for shaving to protect skin:

Shave after showering so that the skin is hot, has been steamed and prepared for a shave

Use a shaving brush to lift the hairs off the skin

Shave with something lubricating like shaving foam or shower gel

Always shave in the direction of travel of the hairs

articles.title: How much rest should flight attendants get? New proposal ignites fight in the skies
articles.summary: A new FAA proposal would override state meal and rest break laws for flight attendants, but major airline unions say it lacks federal guarantees. An aviation industry expert weighed in.
articles.body: A federal proposal that could change meal and rest-break rules for flight attendants is drawing opposition from major airline unions even as aviation experts applaud the plan. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is proposing a nationwide rule that would prevent state and local governments from setting their own meal and rest-break requirements for flight attendants and pilots. Instead, federal aviation rules would apply — according to the agency's proposed rule document. HIGHER FARES COULD SLAM FLIGHT PASSENGERS TO POPULAR REGION AS AIRLINES SHIFT COSTS: 'NOT A FAN' The proposal would affect existing state protections, including meal and rest requirements that have applied to some California-based flight attendants, the document states. Under California law, employees generally must receive a 30-minute meal break when working more than five hours, according to the California Department of Industrial Relations. Employees generally must be relieved of all duties during that period for it to qualify as an off-duty meal break. In its proposal, the FAA argues that different state requirements could interfere with airline operations and conflict with the safety responsibilities of flight attendants. Flight attendants are responsible for handling emergency situations, including fires, medical incidents, evacuations and unruly passengers, according to the FAA document. Requiring a flight attendant to be completely off duty during a break could create a safety risk. The Association of Flight Attendants-CWA (AFA), however, opposes the proposal — arguing that it could remove state protections without establishing a federal guarantee for meal and rest breaks. Requiring a flight attendant to be completely off duty during a break could create a safety risk. The union said some flight attendants already work for hours without adequate opportunities to eat, drink, use the restroom or take care of other basic needs. "While we understand compliance with state laws is not without its challenges, we are far more concerned about the safety impacts of flight attendants working under onerous working conditions," the unions wrote in their joint comments to the FAA. The unions also argued that the proposed protections are "extremely vague" and do not provide enough assurance that airline policies will address both safety and flight attendants' needs. "The proposed rule does little to ensure protections for flight attendants without specific contractual protections," the unions wrote. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The FAA's proposal does not prevent flight attendants from eating, drinking or using the restroom. Instead, airlines would have to allow them to meet those needs while ensuring they remain available for safety responsibilities, according to the document. Michael J. Boyd, president of aviation consulting firm Boyd Group International based in Colorado, told Fox News Digital that, in his opinion, the FAA's approach makes sense given the safety role of flight attendants. Boyd is not connected to the rule developments and expressed his opinion based on his experience in the aviation industry. "They're on duty," Boyd said. "You can't break like that in the middle of the sky." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "They have to be on duty because they're a safety function, just like pilots are, just like firefighters are," he added. Boyd said he does not believe flight attendants would see major changes to their day-to-day work if the proposal is finalized. "Nothing will change," he said. "All they're saying is that state rules do not supersede FAA rules." Boyd also expressed concern that state break requirements could require airlines to add more flight attendants to provide coverage, raising costs. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES Under the current federal system, meal and break arrangements can be addressed through airline policies and collective bargaining agreements, according to the FAA document. Federal rules also require flight attendants to receive 10 consecutive hours of rest between duty periods, the agency noted. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The proposed rule has not been approved or taken effect. Fox News Digital reached out to the FAA and AFA for comment.

articles.title: Por que o Brasil é sempre o primeiro país a falar na ONU? | G1
articles.standfirst: Desde 1955, representante brasileiro é o primeiro a discursar no evento. Saiba quais foram as poucas exceções ao longo dos anos. Presidente Lula discursará na terça (22) de manhã.
articles.summary: Desde 1955, representante brasileiro é o primeiro a discursar no evento. Saiba quais foram as poucas exceções ao longo dos anos. Presidente Lula discursará na terça (22) de manhã.
articles.body:
O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva vai discursar na abertura da Assembleia Geral na Organização das Nações Unidas ( ONU ) , em Nova York, a partir das 10h desta terça-feira (22).

Como é de costume, o líder do Brasil será o primeiro a falar no evento, seguido pelo presidente norte-americano, Donald Trump, representante do país anfitrião.

Embora o Brasil tenha aberto edições anteriores do evento, foi só a partir de 1955 que o país se tornou de fato o primeiro orador das Assembleias Gerais.

🗺️ A Assembleia Geral é um encontro anual que acontece entre os principais governantes e autoridades dos 193 Estados que fazem parte da organização. Vários eventos acontecem durante a reunião — que neste ano tem seis dias de trabalhos.

Há muitas teorias que explicam a origem da tradição.

Uma delas afirma que o posto foi dado aos brasileiros como "prêmio de consolação" por ficar de fora do Conselho de Segurança na ONU.

Outra hipótese é a de que, para evitar aumentar a tensão entre Estados Unidos e União Soviética, que já existia à época dos primeiros eventos, o Brasil foi escolhido por ser considerado neutro.

A explicação mais difundida, no entanto, é outra.

“Em tempos muito antigos, quando ninguém queria falar primeiro , o Brasil sempre se oferecia para falar primeiro. E assim ganhou o direito de falar primeiro na Assembleia Geral”, disse Desmond Parker, chefe de protocolo da ONU, à rádio norte-americana NPR em 2010.

O principal encontro é chamado de "Debate Geral" , que começa nesta terça-feira.

Apesar do nome, não existe de fato um debate entre as nações. Cada país tem o direito de fazer um discurso para apresentar seu ponto de vista sobre o tema do encontro e a situação global.

Quando o Brasil não falou primeiro na Assembleia Geral?

Desde a 10ª sessão em 1955, o Brasil falou primeiro e os Estados Unidos falaram em segundo, com algumas exceções. São elas:

Na 38ª (1983) e na 39ª (1984) sessões, os Estados Unidos falaram primeiro e o Brasil falou em segundo.

Na 71ª sessão, em 20 de setembro de 2016, o Chade falou em segundo lugar devido ao atraso na chegada do presidente dos EUA.

Na 73ª sessão, em 25 de setembro de 2018, o Equador falou em segundo lugar devido ao atraso na chegada do presidente Donald Trump.

Qual é a ordem dos oradores na Assembleia Geral?

Presidente Lula na Assembleia Geral da ONU de 2024 — Foto: Ricardo Stuckert/PR

Após a abertura da reunião pelo presidente da Assembleia Geral, a ordem dos oradores é:

Antonio Guterres, secretário-geral da ONU;

Annalena Baerbock, presidente da Assembleia Geral e ex-ministra das relações exteriores da Alemanha;

A partir daí, a lista é baseada na hierarquia e, geralmente, por ordem de chegada .

Os chefes de Estado falam primeiro, seguidos pelos vice-chefes de Estado e príncipes herdeiros, chefes de governo, ministros e chefes de baixo escalão de uma delegação.

As Nações Unidas foram formadas em 1945, com 51 membros originais e desde então cresceram para 193 membros.

Líderes de dois Estados observadores não-membros – a Santa Sé e o estado da Palestina – e uma entidade observadora com condição especial, a União Europeia, também podem falar.

Os líderes são solicitados a manter um limite de tempo voluntário de 15 minutos, embora esse número possa variar.

articles.title: Mali marks independence amid a worsening security crisis
articles.summary: The 66th anniversary comes as armed groups expand their reach and the government struggles to secure key supply routes.
articles.body:
Bamako, Mali – In Bamako, a fuel blockade has exposed the vulnerability of supply routes into the capital. In the north, separatist and armed groups have increasingly coordinated against the state, while the government faces questions over how much territory it can effectively control.

On September 10, less than two weeks before Mali’s independence anniversary, the Al Qaeda-affiliated armed group Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimeen (JNIM) attacked an army camp in Dioura in central Mali.

The attack followed an April offensive in which JNIM and the Tuareg-led Azawad Liberation Front (FLA), which seeks greater autonomy or independence for northern Mali, coordinated attacks on military and strategic sites in Bamako, Kati, Mopti, Gao and Kidal.

Defence Minister Sadio Camara was killed in the attacks, which exposed the vulnerability of government forces in several parts of the country.

The April offensive followed months of pressure on the capital’s supply lines. Since September 2025, JNIM has targeted fuel tankers and highways carrying fuel from Senegal and Ivory Coast, causing severe shortages in Bamako and disrupting electricity supplies and schooling.

On September 14, more than 900 fuel tankers entered Bamako under military escort, according to the Malian government. But the need to protect such a major operation illustrates the vulnerability of the routes connecting Bamako to its neighbours.

The government seized power in a coup in 2020, promising to restore security. The disruption of vital supply routes, however, has highlighted the difficulty of protecting access to the capital across a vast country.

Northern Mali has long been at the centre of Tuareg demands for greater autonomy or independence. What has changed is the degree of coordination between JNIM and the FLA in confronting the government, despite their different long-term objectives.

Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at Control Risks, told Al Jazeera that the relationship presents a challenge to the military government’s effort to consolidate control over the country’s territory.

“The alliance between JNIM and FLA poses a threat to the government’s consolidation of national territory, which is a key goal of the military. Periodic confrontations between the JNIM-FLA coalition and government forces will continue to undermine a political settlement to the violence,” she said.

Ochieng warned that both sides could harden their positions.

“There is a risk of hardline stances both by the military government and armed groups that will pose a challenge in re-establishing a peace deal between the two sides,” she said.

She said Mali was likely to continue receiving diplomatic and security support from Algeria, its Alliance of Sahel States (AES) partners (Burkina Faso and Niger), and even Senegal and Togo, representing the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). She said that support could delay a deeper security crisis.

The April offensive showed the extent of that coordination, despite the groups’ different objectives. JNIM seeks to impose its interpretation of Islamic law, while the FLA is rooted in Tuareg separatist demands for autonomy and independence.

The two groups have cooperated before, including in 2012 and 2024, but their alliances have broken down over territorial and ideological differences.

Sovereignty rhetoric outpaces control on the ground

Mali has turned away from former regional and international partners and built new alliances around greater national sovereignty.

Mali’s government has framed its withdrawal from these institutions as an assertion of sovereignty. But Abubakar Abubakar Usman, a senior lecturer in international and strategic studies at the University of Malaysia, said Mali’s growing reliance on Russia complicates that argument.

“Mali’s exit from these institutions therefore looks less like an assertion of independence and more like a switching of alliances, from a Western-aligned security order to a Russian-aligned one,” Usman said.

Mali’s withdrawal from ECOWAS alongside Burkina Faso and Niger took effect in January 2025. Human Rights Watch said the withdrawal raised concerns over victims’ access to the ECOWAS Court in cases involving alleged rights abuses.

The three countries have instead strengthened the AES, while Mali has deepened its military relationship with Russia. The Wagner Group’s paramilitary role has been taken over by Russia’s Africa Corps, which operates under the Russian defence ministry.

But the security situation has continued to deteriorate.

The April offensive reached sites near the capital and pushed Russian and Malian forces out of positions in the north. The September attack in Dioura showed that armed groups can still inflict heavy losses on government forces.

In September 2025, Mali announced its withdrawal from the International Criminal Court (ICC), alongside Burkina Faso and Niger. Mali’s formal withdrawal began in June and will take a year. The ICC says withdrawal does not remove obligations while a country remains a member or affect matters already under consideration.

Rights groups have also documented abuses by armed groups, Malian forces and allied Russian fighters. Human Rights Watch said in June that civilians had suffered serious abuses by multiple sides since fighting intensified in April.

The security challenge also extends beyond Mali’s borders.

The AES has established a joint security framework, but each member is facing its own armed conflicts. In Niger, JNIM and Islamic State-linked fighters are competing and fighting, while violence has also placed pressure on neighbouring Benin and Togo.

What independence looks like from Bamako

UNHCR estimated that more than 400,000 people were internally displaced in Mali in June. Gao, Mopti, Menaka and Timbuktu are among the regions hosting significant displaced populations, while the International Organization for Migration (IOM) has identified large displacement sites and continued arrivals in Mopti.

Farming and herding communities are dealing with insecurity, competition over resources and disrupted services. Limited state institutions and the presence of armed groups and local conflicts further complicate the government’s authority.

The government has restored fuel supplies to Bamako, but armed groups can still disrupt key routes and attack military positions.

For residents of the capital, the anniversary arrives with unease.

One Malian resident, who asked not to be identified for safety reasons, described a gap between the government’s language and the reality faced by people on the ground.

“We want to celebrate Independence Day, but there is a lot of anxiety this year. The attacks on the army camp in Dioura have reminded everyone that the security situation is still very fragile,” the resident said.

“We hear the government saying that the army is carrying out operations and that the situation is under control, but people are asking themselves what ‘under control’ really means, especially when armed groups can still carry out attacks of this scale.

“We want to believe that things are improving, but after everything that has happened recently, there is still a lot of uncertainty about where the country is heading.”

articles.title: Maryland hunter's alleged mistake leaves Delaware mother dead
articles.summary: A hunter faces manslaughter charges after allegedly mistaking a woman who was walking through a field for a deer while he was hunting in Delaware.
articles.body: A Maryland hunter is accused of fatally shooting a woman after mistaking her for a deer while she walked through a Delaware field with her children, according to state police. Walter Moorhead, 74, was arrested for manslaughter and other charges after he shot Santos Maria Chilel Soto, 39, on Friday evening in Ellendale, Delaware, State Police said in a press release. Soto was walking through an open field with a man and two children at around 7:40 p.m. as Moorhead was hunting deer from a ground blind, which is a camouflaged structure used by hunters to hide from the sight of game animals. MANHUNT UNDERWAY IN CALIFORNIA AFTER ARMED SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY POINTS GUN AT PEOPLE, SHOOTS AT OFFICERS According to police, Moorhead believed he saw a deer and fired his rifle, striking Soto. State troopers responded to the scene and provided life-saving medical care before Soto was rushed to a local hospital, where she was later pronounced dead. Moorhead was was slapped with multiple felony charges — manslaughter recklessly causing the death of another person, possession of a firearm during the commission of a felony and three counts of first-degree reckless endangerment. SUSPECT IN DEATHS OF 5 FOUND DEAD AFTER COPS UNCOVER GRIM SCENE AT RURAL PROPERTY OUTSIDE PORTLAND He was released from custody after posting a $43,000 cash bond. The incident remains under investigation. Soto was described as a mother of five children and a "beloved" aunt, according to a GoFundMe page. "Maria’s family is now facing the overwhelming pain of this sudden loss while also trying to make sure she is laid to rest with dignity," the fundraiser reads. "This heartbreaking situation has placed a heavy financial burden on the family at a time when they are grieving deeply." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The fundraiser was launched to help the family cover funeral services and the cost of sending her body to Guatemala. Roughly $12,000 has been raised as of Monday evening.

articles.title: Russia’s parliamentary election results were predictable but what comes next matters
articles.summary: The result of Russia’s tightly controlled parliamentary election was never in serious doubt: a resounding win for the ruling United Russia party, which fervently backs President Vladimir Putin and Russia’s war in Ukraine.
articles.body: The result of Russia’s tightly controlled parliamentary election was never in serious doubt: a resounding win for the ruling United Russia party, which fervently backs President Vladimir Putin and Russia’s war in Ukraine. The fact that genuine political opposition to the Kremlin and its costly war has been effectively silenced in recent years made the outcome of the ballot – the first parliamentary elections since 2021, before the Ukraine war began – all the more inevitable. The only remaining opposition party calling for an end to the war, Yabloko, was barred from taking part. Even before the vote, Putin told Russians the election would showcase national unity and that “millions of people are backing our fighters” – a sign of his confidence in the result. The nationwide election has also been used to underline that Russia – unlike Ukraine – is prepared to hold a vote in wartime, which may curry favor with US President Donald Trump, who has criticized Kyiv’s constitutional ban on elections during martial law. But what was always far less certain than the outcome of this Russian vote, and potentially more significant, is how a fresh veneer of political support would be used and what course of action the Kremlin will push next. The mere staging of a nationwide vote – across 11 Russian time zones and in annexed regions occupied by Russian forces in Ukraine – has been cast in Russia as a sign of normalcy, which is important to the Kremlin as it grapples with an escalating war. Amid soaring casualties on the front lines, mounting economic hardship and rising public anxiety, the reality of what Russia calls its Special Military Operation in Ukraine is increasingly being felt. Yet with the relentless Ukrainian drone strikes – including the biggest wave ever launched against the Moscow region as voting took place this weekend – the Kremlin has been at pains to reassure Russians that life goes on largely unaffected. But that reassurance may become harder to sustain as pressure builds on Russia’s war machine, and the Kremlin vows to press ahead with achieving its military objectives in Ukraine, whatever the cost. One of the sharpest fears, as the Kremlin pushes to break the frontline deadlock, is that the Kremlin will use its claim of a fresh mandate to launch a new round of forced mobilization into the depleting ranks of the Russian military. A chaotic partial mobilization in September 2022 saw about 300,000 men called up, sparking widespread anger and the panicked exodus through gridlocked border checkpoints of hundreds of thousands of Russians desperate to escape the draft. The Kremlin has since tightened border controls, making it harder to flee. But it has also dismissed outright concerns of a repeat as scaremongering, with Putin himself categorically denying there is a general call-up plan, lambasting the speculation as “complete nonsense” and an “information attack on Russia.” Given that personal insistence, the election – in which 49 veterans of the Ukraine war were elected – is more likely to be used as evidence that Russia rewards its soldiers with plum political jobs, as a means of boosting voluntary recruitment. Still, some cautious Russians of military age, fearing a U-turn, are leaving the country just in case, mindful that the dire need for fresh troops could eventually outweigh the Kremlin’s urge to avoid public outrage. There are heightened concerns of other measures in the offing too – from a renewed military push in Ukraine to further tightening of social and economic controls at home – by a Kremlin that feels like the resounding parliamentary election result has delivered renewed authority to act.

articles.title: ‘Looksmaxxing’ influencer Clavicular charged with rape in Massachusetts
articles.summary: The “looksmaxxing” personality known as Clavicular has been charged with rape in Massachusetts, online court records show.
articles.body: The “looksmaxxing” personality known as Clavicular has been charged with rape in Massachusetts, online court records show. The charges listed against Clavicular, 20, whose real name is Braden Peters, are one count of rape, one count of drugging someone for sexual intercourse, and one count of procuring liquor for someone under 21 years old, according to the records. The charges were filed Sept. 8, and the alleged offenses occurred May 23, 2025, the records indicate. More details about the allegations were not immediately available. Online court records did not show an attorney who could speak on his behalf Monday night. The Bulwark first reported the charges. A representative for Clavicular, Mitchell Jackson, said the outlet was “exaggerating” in its report and that Clavicular had not been served with an arrest warrant. “Braden Peters has not been physically served. As usual the Bulwark is exaggerating,” Jackson said in a text message Monday night. An email to the general mailbox of The Bulwark seeking comment was not immediately returned late Monday. An arraignment was scheduled for Oct. 14, according to the court records. Clavicular has gained internet fame — and notoriety — for a trend among young men known as “looksmaxxing,” which Meriam-Webster Dictionary recently called, “The practice of taking one or more sometimes extreme or dangerous measures intended to increase one’s physical attractiveness.” He has been known for “bone smashing,” or using a hammer to intentionally break facial bones so they grow back stronger or looking better. The trend has been called potentially unhealthy and dangerous by experts. Clavicular in April was sued by a teenage influencer in Florida who accused him of battery. Aleksandra Vasilevna Mendoza, who online is known as Alorah or Alorah Ziva, filed a lawsuit in Miami-Dade County that alleged that in 2025 he arranged for her to go to Cape Cod, Massachusetts, gave her vodka until she was drunk, and then had sex with her while she was intoxicated, NBC South Florida reported. Online court records do not indicate whether the charges of rape, drugging or procurement of alcohol to someone under 21 are related to the allegations in the lawsuit. Clavicular’s attorney at the time said that he denies the allegations and “intends to vigorously defend himself,” according to the news station. Clavicular and two other people in April were also charged in Florida with shooting at an alligator. He and another person pleaded no contest to unlawfully discharging a firearm in public and were given six months of probation and ordered to serve 20 hours of community service, according to NBC South Florida. He was also hospitalized in April in Miami after a suspected overdose. He said in a livestream at the time after being released from the hospital that, “I ain’t gonna be doing any more substances for a little while, hopefully for forever.”

articles.title: Mumbai Coastal Road tragedy: BMW driver had faced 2 prior cases over drunken brawl, speeding
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Shanay Gajjar, the 21-year-old student who was driving the BMW that plunged 70 feet down from the Coastal Road flyover early Sunday near Lotus.
articles.body: MUMBAI: Shanay Gajjar, the 21-year-old student who was driving the BMW that plunged 70 feet down from the Coastal Road flyover early Sunday near Lotus Jetty, and who died in the fatal mishap along with two others, previously faced two cases registered by the city police. In March, Gamdevi police registered a case against him for alleged dangerous driving and endangering the lives of others. Last month, Bandra police filed a case against him and three of his friends for allegedly engaging in a drunken brawl with police outside a pub.On Sunday, the BMW was travelling from Marine Drive towards Haji Ali on the northbound carriageway when the tragedy occurred. Police identified the deceased as Dhairya Sheth (17), Aditya Jaskania (19) and Shanay Gajjar, who was driving the car that belonged to his family. Aditya Oswal (23), who suffered multiple injuries in the accident, is in the hospital.Tardeo police on Monday registered a case against Gajjar for causing death by negligence, rash driving and dangerous driving. All the victims were from Ahmedabad.CCTV footage showed the BMW speeding. The impact was such that one of the victi­ms was thrown around 20 feet from the car and another was found outside it. Police said Ga­­jjar was still partly inside the vehicle, with his leg on the accelerator.In Aug, Bandra police had filed a case against Gajjar and his three friends for obstructing a public servant in the discharge of public functions and under the Maharashtra Prohibition Act. They were served notices and allowed to leave. Police are yet to file a chargesheet in the case.Police constable Baban Sagare alleged the four were caught fighting after partying at a pub on the night of Aug 19-20. They initially left after police intervened, but later began to argue among themselves on the road. Police alleged that after they intervened again, under the influence of alcohol, the four argued with the cops and then charged at them when asked to leave. All four were taken to Bandra police station, where they allegedly caused a disturbance, and later at Bhabha Hospital where they were taken for medical tests. A police officer said they refused the medical examination and blood tests, and the medical officer recorded their refusal.Earlier, on March 29, Omkar Shirke (29), a businessman and resident of Tardeo in central Mumbai, lodged an FIR against the driver of a BMW car bearing the number DD 01 C 6302. Shirke told police that on the night of March 28, while he was going towards his residence, a speeding BMW passed by dangerously close to him. He later spotted the car near Mahalaxmi temple and questioned the driver who gave evasive replies. Police then issued a notice to Gajjar. articles.title: North Korea reports new missile test designed to give enemy ‘incurable headache’
articles.summary: North Korea said it successfully tested a new weapon showcasing “ultra-modern defense technology” on Sunday, state media reported Tuesday.
articles.body: SEOUL, South Korea — North Korea said it successfully tested a new weapon showcasing “ultra-modern defense technology” on Sunday, in a launch overseen by leader Kim Jong Un, who praised progress in strengthening the country’s war readiness, state media reported Tuesday. Kim said the test, conducted by North Korea’s Missile Administration, demonstrated a significant development in the country’s armed forces’ ability to fight and that “the enemy will know better what such progress means without any explanation.” “He affirmed that such reality would give the enemy an incurable headache and a very cruel and unavoidable blow,” Kim was quoted as saying. The KCNA report did not specify the type of weapon tested. Photographs released by KCNA showed Kim, accompanied by his teenage daughter, inspecting a screen displaying a map of the country’s east coast and the “flight trajectory” of Hwasongpho-11-ma-1, which is likely part of a series of short-range ballistic missiles being upgraded by Pyongyang. NK News, a Seoul-based website specializing in North Korea, said the projectile appeared to be an upgraded variant of a missile equipped with a hypersonic glide vehicle. Mounting a glide vehicle on a missile means the warhead can maneuver to evade anti-missile defenses and also potentially be launched partially into orbit. Hypersonic missiles are among a range of weapons that Kim has called for development to upgrade its nuclear capabilities. The South Korean military said Sunday that North Korea fired two short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast. The test came days after Pyongyang accused the United States of raising tensions on the Korean Peninsula through a series of military drills. On Monday, the foreign ministers of South Korea, Japan and the U.S. met on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York to agree to coordinate closely for peace, stability and denuclearization on the Korean Peninsula, according to Seoul’s foreign ministry.

articles.title: Will shut Iranian flights from Wednesday: US new arm-twist move against Tehran
articles.summary: US News: US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said Iranian airlines could \"effectively be shut out of global operations\" from Wednesday and threatened foreign c.
articles.body: US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said Iranian airlines could "effectively be shut out of global operations" from Wednesday and threatened foreign companies providing services to Tehran’s aviation sector with secondary sanctions.Bessent on Monday said, “on September 23, all the Iranian airlines will be shut down around the world”.“If they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets, or you will be knocked out of the dollar system,” Bessent said, according to Al Jazeera.The warning comes as the Trump administration expands its sanctions campaign aimed at restricting Iran’s access to international financial and commercial networks.Earlier this month, the US treasury department imposed sanctions on additional Iranian airlines as well as companies outside Iran accused of supporting Tehran’s aviation sector.Iran’s aviation industry has already faced years of US sanctions, limiting Iranian carriers’ ability to acquire new aircraft and access spare parts and maintenance services.The latest measures are part of a broader US sanctions regime targeting Iran’s economy, including its energy, shipping, technology, gold and digital-asset sectors. Secondary sanctions can subject foreign companies doing business with sanctioned Iranian entities to restrictions on access to the US financial system.Bessent’s comments came a day after talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, ahead of a planned meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.China is a key economic partner and diplomatic supporter of Iran, making Beijing’s cooperation significant to Washington’s efforts to restrict Tehran’s access to international finance.According to Al Jazeera, Bessent said Chinese officials had been “very engaged” in discussions over the US pressure campaign. He also said Washington was holding positive talks with Chinese financial authorities, including People’s Bank of China Governor Pan Gongsheng, on compliance with US sanctions targeting Iran.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
